chunks: Ground plane vs ground traces. The question: What are the tradeoffs between using a ground plane vs ground traces to connect all ground potentials?
There are two ways to distribute ground on a board. A ground plane is a solid copper layer that every ground connection drops into through a via.
Ground traces are routed connections, such as a chain, a star or a grid. The plane has far lower resistance and inductance and keeps each signal's return loop small.
Traces make sense on cheap one- or two-layer boards, or where you want a deliberately separate return.
Imagine a neighborhood where everyone must walk home. With a plane, it is an open field, and each person walks a short, direct route home.
With ground traces, it is one narrow lane that all the neighbors share, so the last house on the lane has everyone else's foot traffic in the way.
The analogy is loose: a fast return current follows the path right under its own signal.
With a daisy chain, segment R g1 carries all three currents (300 milliamps, 15 millivolts), R g2 carries two (200 milliamps, 10 millivolts) and R g3 one (100 milliamps, 5 millivolts).
Each node's ground sits above the source ground by the sum of upstream drops, and any change in I 1 moves G2 and G3.
Daisy chain: loads connected in a row on one ground trace, so each later load sees the earlier loads' currents ("Ground potential differences across a board").
Star grounding: a separate trace from each load to one common point ("Star grounding"). Ground grid: ground traces in both directions tied together with vias, a middle option.
Loop area: the area between a signal and its return. Radiation grows with it.
Common-impedance coupling: voltage made in a shared conductor that appears in another circuit's reference ("What PCB grounding is and why it matters").
Put three 100 milliamps loads on a daisy-chained ground trace, with 50 milliohms per segment. The first segment carries all 300 milliamps, so it drops 15 millivolts.
The second carries 200 milliamps and adds 10 millivolts, so the second load's ground sits 25 millivolts up. The third adds 5 millivolts, so it sits 30 millivolts up.
Any change in the first load's current moves the other two. On a plane the same currents spread out and the drops are tens of times smaller. That is the whole idea.
"A ground plane gives much lower impedance than ground traces: about 0.
5 milliohms per square and sub-nanohenry spreading, versus roughly 190 milliohms and 140 nanohenries for a 100 mm thin trace.
It also puts the return directly under each signal, so loops are small, and it avoids the common-impedance buildup of a daisy chain.
Traces cost less and let you force a deliberate single-point return, so they're right for one- or two-layer boards and for things like a shunt measurement.
Otherwise I use a plane, or a ground grid as a compromise."
